data.title: Malý Manín – a hillfort above the Manín gorge
data.excerpt: Malý Manín (812 m) rises on the left bank of the Váh and forms part of the Manín gorge. Terraces on its upland plateau have yielded occupation from the Late Bronze Age through the Early and Late Iron Age to the Roman period, together with ramparts, a pincer-shaped gate, a serpentine access road and an estimated 50 to 60 houses.

children.text: Malý Manín is part of the Strážov hills; it rises on the left bank of the Váh in the middle Váh region. It forms part of the Manín gorge. The elevation of Malý Manín is 812 m above sea level.

In 2000, occupation of several periods was identified on some of the terraces of the upland plateau, namely from the Late Bronze Age through the Early and Late Iron Age to the Roman period. After a longer period of observation the fortification was identified – ramparts, a pincer-shaped entrance gate, an access road of serpentine form, in places 3–4 m wide – the only entrance into the whole enclosure, and presumed cisterns for collecting rainwater.

The area of the hillfort is more than 8 ha, its length approximately 630 m and its width 80–120 m. Across the whole area of the hillfort there are terraces, and in them fragments of pottery – sherds, predominantly of the Lusatian and Púchov cultures, fragments of loom weights, spindle whorls made from fragments of graphite pottery, a larger quantity of burnt clay – daub (the filling between the timbers of a dwelling), and various metal objects – an iron axe, part of a bronze bracelet, an iron spur and others.

It is assumed that the site was occupied as early as 1000 BC. In its area it was among the largest in the surroundings of Považská Bystrica. The objects found were identified by specialists: Jozef Moravčík, graduate historian, and Mgr. Róbert Majský, archaeologist of the Museum of Local History in Považská Bystrica.
From the fragments of pottery found it is possible to determine the period of manufacture, the shape and size of the vessel, the material from which and the way in which the pottery was made.

The oldest sherds can be dated to the Late Bronze Age, around 1000 BC. The pottery was handmade, not thrown on the potter's wheel. The shape of the vessel was bulbous, considerably widened in the middle, with the upper rim slightly everted. The decoration – in most cases horizontal lines, between them circles, sometimes impressions made with a finger – dimples. Usually there were two or four small lugs opposite each other, and as a rule the decoration was in the upper part of the vessel. For the most part a fine-grained material such as fine sand was used in manufacture. In the later period, in the Early Iron Age, the shape of the pottery changed slightly, more coarse-grained material was used and bosses were often used instead of lugs. In both periods the Lusatian culture was present. It lasted until the 3rd century BC. The pottery of the Púchov culture was considerably different, in the first place in its decoration: vertical lines were used, the upper rim was flanged, crushed limestone was used in the mixture, and since it was made on the potter's wheel, vessels of larger dimensions – storage jars – were produced; part of the pottery was made of graphite. For the making of loom weights a clayey soil was used, slightly fired, of pyramidal shape, with a hole in the upper part for hanging. The weights were used predominantly in the Late Iron Age in the Púchov culture.

In the Late Bronze Age a dwelling was built predominantly of posts sunk into the ground, about half a metre apart and interwoven with rods. According to the objects found, the rods were smeared with clay – daub – mixed with chaff. The evidence for this is the impressions in the daub. Judging by the terrace, the house was approximately 5 m long and around 3.5 m wide, slightly sunk into the ground and covered with straw or reeds. In the earlier period these houses, according to the literature, had no windows, only small openings for air. The door was probably formed by a hanging animal skin. In the middle of the feature there was usually a hearth, and along the edges some kind of beds.

children.text: Farm buildings or sties were probably also attached to the dwellings. A path, lined with round stones from the Váh, evidently led to the dwelling. A length of lining about 1.5 m long was uncovered. It is estimated that there were about 50 to 60 such houses on Malý Manín. An interesting structure at the site was a pit, according to archaeologists probably a cistern for collecting rainwater. At its upper edge it is 15 m wide and in the middle 1.5 m deep. It lies at the lowest point on almost every side. Another interesting structure is the pincer-shaped gate, which is flanked on either side by earthen ramparts. The access road was of serpentine form, in places 2 to 4 m wide. We assume that the hillfort was abandoned in the first century AD, in the Roman period. More knowledge would be made possible by a specialist archaeological survey, which would reveal further unknown circumstances.
